messages.subject: Re: outfit.z seems wrong
messages.body_plain:
I'm not entirely sure what to make of this since the eRm package appears to follow the same format that mirt does in calculating these statistics. Copied from there code we can see that the two implementation are exactly the same (independently written, might I add, since I didn't use their code as a reference):

############################
i.outfitMSQ <- ifit/idf

  qsq.outfitMSQ <- (colSums(Cmat/Vmat^2, na.rm=TRUE)/idf^2) - 1/idf
  q.outfitMSQ <- sqrt(qsq.outfitMSQ)

  isumVmat<-colSums(Vmat)
  i.infitMSQ <- colSums(sq.res*Vmat, na.rm = TRUE)/isumVmat

  qsq.infitMSQ <- colSums(Cmat-Vmat^2, na.rm=TRUE)/isumVmat^2
  q.infitMSQ <- sqrt(qsq.infitMSQ)

  i.outfitZ <- (i.outfitMSQ^(1/3) - 1)*(3/q.outfitMSQ)+(q.outfitMSQ/3) # corr. rh 2011-06-15
  i.infitZ  <- (i.infitMSQ^(1/3)  - 1)*(3/q.infitMSQ) +(q.infitMSQ/3)  # hint from rainer alexandrowicz

############################

In fact, comparing the two models gives very close results, the differences being a) the estimator (MML versus CML) and b) how extreme response patterns are handled. Here's a quick comparison use mirt version 0.7.4 and eRm version 0.15-1:

############################

> library(eRm)
> res <- RM(raschdat1)
> p.res <- person.parameter(res)
> erm <- itemfit(p.res)
>
> library(mirt)
Loading required package: stats4
Loading required package: lattice

Follow the mirt package on github: https://github.com/philchalmers/mirt

Attaching package: ‘mirt’

The following object is masked from ‘package:eRm’:

    itemfit, personfit

> mod <- mirt(raschdat1, 1, 'Rasch')
Iteration: 8, Log-Lik: -1752.855, Max-Change: 0.00010
> mirt <- itemfit(mod, method = 'ML')
> vals <- data.frame(mirt$outfit, erm$i.outfitMSQ, mirt$z.outfit, erm$i.outfitZ,
+               mirt$infit, erm$i.infitMSQ, mirt$z.infit, erm$i.infitZ)
> head(vals)
   mirt.outfit erm.i.outfitMSQ mirt.z.outfit erm.i.outfitZ mirt.infit erm.i.infitMSQ mirt.z.infit erm.i.infitZ
I1   0.8192734       0.8195980   -0.75364295   -0.75162768  0.9556446      0.9559850   -0.3011689   -0.2982931
I2   0.9975447       0.9975391    0.02666868    0.02662913  1.0682389      1.0682265    0.8233076    0.8231748
I3   0.9903701       0.9903065   -0.01429445   -0.01473404  0.9497869      0.9497646   -0.5189905   -0.5192427
I4   0.8421997       0.8422234   -0.84528599   -0.84501688  0.8883034      0.8883505   -1.1101270   -1.1095593
I5   1.0893675       1.0889196    0.41163239    0.41016310  1.1179150      1.1175912    0.8700886    0.8682042
I6   1.2198264       1.2198075    1.58353939    1.58342223  1.1722011      1.1721681    1.9787836    1.9784730
> max(abs(vals[,c(1,3,5,7)] - vals[,c(2,4,6,8)]))
[1] 0.01383972

############################

So the ultimate question comes to this: who do we think is more right, Winsteps or eRm? Maybe contacting the Winsteps crew or Patrick Mair would help clear up the issue.

Phil

messages.subject: Missing Data and item-person ft
messages.body_plain:
Hi Phil,

i realized that itemfit, personfit and fitIndices are not calculated with missing data.
Is imputation the only way around this?
I am comparing Rasch to other IRT models and have plenty of missing data (the "non-aplicable" response was coded as missing)

Thanks,

Carolina

messages.subject: Re: Missing Data and item-person ft
messages.body_plain:
Hi Carolina,

Unfortunately most if not all of fit statistics are ill defined when missing data are present, so complete data is really the only option here.

However, instead of an imputation approach you could try fitting the data with the missing response data to obtain FIML estimates, create a new smaller dataset which omits the missing response cases, and form a new non-estimated model with the FIML estimated coefficients on the smaller dataset that contains only complete observations. Using this model will allow you to use the functions that you mentioned. I'm not sure how kosher this is in the literature but I think it's justifiable if item, person, and model diagnostics really are important, and at least should give valid results for cases with non-missing data.

Otherwise if you are just interested in nested model comparisons likelihood ratio tests are still valid, along with their information theoretic counterparts (AIC, BIC, etc.) through the anova() generic. Hope that helps!

Phil
